prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, enabling optical timekeeping and precision tests at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: The optical lattice clock is a clear invention in the sense I take the mandate to require. Katori's magic-wavelength lattice idea made it possible to interrogate many neutral atoms at once without the trap perturbing the clock transition, and Ye's group then showed what the idea could do, taking systematic uncertainty to the 10^-18 range and exploring the many-body, spin-resolved regime. It is a tool that opens a door to measurements that could not be made before: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, tests of the constancy of fundamental constants, searches for new physics, and a route to a redefinition of the second. It is experimentally verified by several independent laboratories with routine international comparisons, and the attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist, with a two-person division between invention and leading realisation. In my own opening ballot I put B009 first, but six of eight members rank B008 in their top five and five in their top three, so I now see it as the strongest shared case, and I do not want my personal field to drive the outcome.
statement.case_against: The lattice clock builds on prizes already awarded for the frequency comb (2005) and for ion control (2012), so one can argue the novelty is incremental, a better clock rather than a new phenomenon. The SI redefinition of the second has not happened, so the societal payoff is still prospective. Other laboratories (SYRTE, PTB, NIST, and Sr and Yb groups) contributed important realisations, and any two-name credit must draw the line around the invention and its leading demonstration. There is also a fair question about whether a technology-heavy precision-measurement result is a discovery or an application.

responses.point: Ranks B008 first because the magic-wavelength lattice with many atoms probed in parallel took uncertainty to the 1e-18 level and opens relativistic geodesy, constants tests and dark-matter searches, and that two laureates are a clean configuration with other groups' implementations left aside.
responses.response: I agree on the substance and on the attribution line. Katori's concept and first Sr lattice demonstration are the original invention, and Ye's work is the decisive realisation. I would qualify one thing. Where you describe the clock as opening observation regimes, the committee should be careful to cite only verified results such as the redshift measurements and the record uncertainty budgets, not future prospects such as dark-matter sensitivity. The citation should rest on what has actually been demonstrated.

responses.point: Ranks B008 first and notes that the committee might want to wait for the SI redefinition of the second to complete the story, and that ion-clock groups are a possible attribution question.
responses.response: I would not wait for the redefinition. The Nobel criterion is a verified invention or discovery, not an administrative decision by the metrology community, and the performance is already confirmed by independent labs. On the ion-clock question I think 2012 honoured control of single quantum systems, which is a different invention, so I consider the overlap manageable. You are better placed than I am to judge the atomic-structure and systematic-shift physics, so I would like you to say whether any key systematic, such as the lattice light shift or blackbody radiation, was established by a group outside the two credited names.

responses.point: Ranks B049 first as a new state of matter with a clean theory plus experiment trio of Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, with high lasting influence and stable interpretation.
responses.response: I rank B049 fourth and I take the physics seriously, but I do not think the trio is as clean as you describe. Molenkamp's HgTe observation followed the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal, which is not in the credited set, and Johansson, Lindroth and Mehlig all flag that omission as a real attribution problem. Since I am committed to being absolutely sure that the people credited did the original work, I would hesitate to give this prize on a historical record that leaves out a decisive step. I would be persuaded if you can show that the Kane-Mele Z2 theory and the HgTe experiment stand as a complete discovery on their own.

responses.point: Ranks circuit QED first and B008 second, but flags that a cQED prize so soon after the 2025 superconducting circuits prize might look repetitive, and that Girvin and Huard have claims.
responses.response: I think your own caution about the 2025 overlap and the Girvin and Huard attribution is right, and it is a reason I keep B012 below B008. You also raised a conflict of interest for yourself as a member close to that community. I would ask you to say plainly whether you intend to recuse from the cQED discussion. On B008 I appreciate that you rank it second with a clean two-name credit.

responses.point: Ranks the experimental Higgs discovery first as the clearest experimental clue from nature in modern fundamental physics, with ATLAS and CMS leaders Gianotti, Della Negra and Virdee proposed.
responses.response: I share your view on importance, and I ranked it second myself. My difficulty is the one you name. Four credited founders and leaders for two collaborations of thousands cannot be reduced to three without dropping someone, and my own trio differs from yours. I do not think leadership roles map reliably onto the people who did the original work, so I would like to see an argument that does not rest on spokesperson titles. Until the committee can agree on the three names, I regard B008 as the safer configuration, but I keep B056 as an alternative.

responses.point: Ranks IceCube first and sees B009 aberration correction as a very good instrument advance that may belong more naturally in a chemistry or materials prize.
responses.response: That is a fair concern about B009 and I tried to flag it in my own opening uncertainties. As the committee's microscopist I have a proximity to this field that I cannot ignore, and it is a reason I should not be the one to decide where electron optics belongs. I also note that you rank B008 third, so you accept its quality. On IceCube, I rated it seventh mainly because the sources of most events remain unidentified and the TXS 0506+056 association has modest significance, but I take your point that the diffuse flux is solid.

uncertainties: Whether independent systematic-shift work, for example on lattice light shifts or blackbody radiation, was established by groups outside Katori and Ye, which would change the attribution.
How much weight the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize should carry against the novelty of the lattice clock.
Whether the committee prefers to wait for the SI redefinition of the second, which I think is not necessary.
Whether B009 belongs in physics at all, and who is owed credit on the STEM-corrector side (Krivanek and collaborators).
statement.conflict_note: As an electron microscopist I have a field-proximity conflict with B009 (spherical-aberration correction in TEM). I ranked it first in my opening ballot and the candidates work in the microscopy community in which I am active, including as President of the IFSM. I therefore propose that I should recuse from deciding that candidate and I do not include it in my preferred configuration. Göran Johansson is a colleague at Chalmers Physics, but I have no personal or institutional connection to Katori, Ye or the other shortlisted candidates that is apparent from my profile.
